Date of pronouncement : 02.08.2018
In re:
Delhi Administration / Food Inspector
Department of Pfa,
Govt. of Nct of Delhi
A-20, Lawrence Road Industrial Area,
Delhi-110035 ...

Complainant
 versus
Sh. Sanjay Kumar
S/o Sh. Nepali Singh
Ajay Kiryana Store, Khasra No.1/24,
Nathupura Road, Near Janta Medical Store,
Burari. Delhi-84
R/o C/o Sh. Jai Parkash Tyagi,
Mangal Bazax, Village Burari,
Delhi-84 ... Accused
Judgment:
1. The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(herein after referred to as Pfa Act), alleging that the accused has violated the provisions of th
e PFA Act and Rules.

2. As per the complaint, on 27.10.07 at about 4 PM, Food Inspector Gian Chand purchased a sample of "Dal Arhar a food article for DA vs Sanjay Kumar analysis from accused Sanjay Kumar from the premises of Ajay Kiryana Store, Khasra No.1/24 Nathupura Road, Near Janta Medical Store, Burari.
Delhi-84 where the said food article was found stored for sale and where accused Sanjay Kumar vendor was found conducting the business of the said food article at the time of sampling.

Approx.
1500 gms. of Dal Arhar was taken from an open tin bearing no label or declaration.
The sample was taken under the supervision/direction of Sh. Yogesh Pratap.
SDM/LHA.
The sample was taken after proper mixing the Dal Arhar with the help of a clean & dry Jhaba by rotating it in all possible directions.
The Food Inspector divided the sample commodity into three equal parts then and there by putting them into three clean and dry glass bottles.

Each sample bottle was separately packed,

1 fastened and sealed according to PFA Act 8.
Rules.
The vendor's signatures were obtained on me LHA slip and wrapper of the sample bottles.
Notice in Form VI was given to Sh. Sanjay Kumar and the price of sample was also given to him vide vendor's receipt dated 27.10.07.
Panchnama too was prepared at the spot.
All the documents prepared by FI were signed by accused Sanjay Kumar and the other witness Sh. J.P. Bhardwaj, FA.
Before starting sample proceedings efforts were made to join public witnesses but none tame forward.
as such Sh. J.P. Bhardwaj. FA was joined as witness.

3. One counter-part of the sample bearing LHA Code Number 41/LHA/19827 was also sent to Public Analyst, Delhi in intact condition and remaining two counterparts were deposited with the SDM/LHA in intact conditions.
Public AnaIyst analysed the sample and found the sample to be adulterated.

The report of Public DA vs Sanjay Kumar Analyst is as follows:
"The sample is adulterated because it is coloured with synthetic colouring matter viz tartrazine".
4.

It is the case of the complainant that accused Sanjay Kumar was the vendor-cum-proprietor of Ajay Kiryana Store, Khasra No.1/24 Nathuputa Road, Near Janta Medical Store, Burari, Delhi-84 at the time of taking sample and as such he is in charge of and responsible for day to day conduct of the business of the said shop.
The vendor did not disclose to the food inspector the name, address and other particulars of the person from whom he had purchased the article of food.
5. Thereafter on completion of investigation, sanction under section 20 of the PFA Act was obtained from the Director PFA.

The complaint was then filed in the court on 07.04.2008 alleging violation of section 2(ia)(j)&(m) and Rule 23 read with Rule 29 of PFA Rules, 1955 as punishable section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act against the accused.
6. As the complaint was filed in writing by a public servant, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused was summoned vide order dated 07.04.2008.

Based on the report of the PA charge was framed against the accused for commission of the offence punishable under section 7/16(1) (a) PFA Act being violation of Section 2(ia)(a)(b)(j)&(m) of PFA Act and Rule 23 read with Rule 28 & 29 of PFA Rules, 1955, to which accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
DA vs Sanjay Kumar 7.

At the trial, the prosecution examined four witness in support of its case i.e. PW-1 FI Gian Chand,
PW-2 SDM/LHA Sh Yogesh Pratap, and PW-3 FA J.P. Bhardwaj.

PW-1 and PW-3 were part of the team that had visited the spot for sample proceedings under the supervision of SDM/LHA Sh.
Yogesh Pratap.

These witness narrated the steps undertaken by them during the sample proceedings, including disclosing their identity, expressing intention to purchase sample for analysis, lifting the sample commodity of "Arhar Dal" 1.50 kg from the vendor for analysis, bearing no label or declaration, taking the sample of Arhar Dal and rotating in all directions, dividing the sample into three equal parts by putting them into three separate clean and dry sample bottles,
separately sealing, packing and marking the same and obtaining signatures of vendor and witnesses.

They also proved the necessary documents including the vendor's receipt Ex.PW- 1/A, Notice Ex.
Da vs Sanjay Kumar on 2 August, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67851671/
2 PW-1/B, Panchnama Ex.PW-1/C.
The accused also made statement Ex.PW1/D alongwith document.

Thereafter, the remaining two counter parts of the sample in intact condition along with two copies of memo of Form VII in a sealed packet were deposited with LHA vide LHA Receipt Ex.PW1/F under intimation that one counterpart of the same has already been deposited with PA vide receipt Ex.PW1/E.
Thereafter, PA Report Ex.PW1/H was received, according to which the sample found adulterated being coloured with synthetic colouring matter tatrazine.

Thereafter the PW-1 FI Shri Gian Chand started the investigations and he sent a letter Ex. PW 1/I to VATO, Ward No. 72 and received its reply stating that the firm Ajay Kiryana Store was not registered in that Ward.

Thereafter after completion of investigation, the entire case file including Public Analyst report DA vs Sanjay Kumar was submitted to Shri Mohan Lal, the then Director, PFA, who after applying his mind gave the consent Ex. PW 1/J.

sentences.text: Thereafter the present complaint Ex. PW 1/K was filed by PW-4 FI D.V. Singh
Then the intimation letter Ex.PW4/A alongwith PA report was sent to accused vide postal registration receipts Ex.PW4/B.
These witnesses were duly cross-examined by Ld. Defence Counsel.
8. Statement of the accused under section 313 CrPC were recorded wherein the accused denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
Thereafter matter was listed for defence evidence.
But the accused has not lead any defence evidence and matter was listed for final arguments.
9. In a criminal case, the burden is on the prosecution to prove its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt by leading positive evidence.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and it has to be necessary discharged by the prosecution itself.

10. It is to be understood that the charge framed against the accused is for violation of section 2(ia)(a),(b) (j) and (m) of the PFA Act read with Rules 23 and 29 of PFA Rules with respect to 'adulteration'.

Under section 2(ia)(a) of PFA Act, the prosecution has to establish that the purchaser had demanded a food article of a specific nature, substance or quality and the article sold was, to his prejudice, either not of the nature, substance or quality demanded, or was not of the nature,
substance or quality which it purported or represented to be.
Section 2(ia)(j) specifically deals with colouring matter which is present other than prescribed or is present beyond DA vs Sanjay Kumar the prescribed limits of variability.

Section 2(ia)(m) of PFA Act deals with situation where the quality or purity of an article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability.
11.The commodity in the present case is Dal Arhar which is food grain and has to be tested as per the standards prescribed for food grains.
It is clear that this article falls in Item A.18.06.09 of Appendix B to the PFA Rules.
Public analysts has applied the same standard to this product.
It is nowhere the stand of the accused that the food article does not fall under this head or that it falls under some other head.
12. It is pertinent to note that PA has found the presence of the synthetic colouring matter Tartrazine which is a totally prohibited item in the sample analysed.

Da vs Sanjay Kumar on 2 August, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67851671/
3 13.
The defence taken by the accused is that the intimation letter has not been served upon him.
The accused has also not exercised his right under section 13(2) PFA Act for getting the sample analysed through CFL.
For this, the arguments are that PA report with intimation letter were never served upon it.

14. As per the scheme of the Act, after a sample (in three counterparts) is lifted by the FI, he is required as per section 11 to send, by the immediately succeeding working day, one counterpart of sample to PA for analysis and deposit the remaining two counterparts with the LHA.
The PA analyses the sample and delivers report to the LHA under section 13 of Act.

Under section DA vs Sanjay Kumar 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused, informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA.
It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and his right cannot be frustrated by the prosecution.
The point to be noted is, that such forwarding of report has to be after the institution of the prosecution in the court and not prior to filing of the case.
Also, the accused has 10 days time from the date of receipt of report to apply to the court.

Again, if so applied, the court requires the LHA to produce counterpart of the sample before it, and upon receipt of such requisition, LHA is required to produce it within 5 days (section 13(2-A) of Act) before the court.
The court then sends the said counterpart to the CFL for analyses, and the Director, CFL is required to send report of analysis within 1 month.
15. At the outset, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused.
PW-4 deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter Ex. PW-4/A through registered post vide receipt Ex.PW-4/B.
The receipt clearly shows the correct address of the accused.
It is pertinent to note that the genuineness of this document has never been questioned by the defence.
It is not the case where no original receipt exists or that the receipt shown to the court was forged or fabricated.
No objection was taken by the defence as to the mode of proof when this document was exhibited.
The correctness of the postal receipt DA vs Sanjay Kumar has not been questioned during cross-examination of PWs.
Not even a single suggestion was given to the witnesses that the postal receipt Ex. PW-1/B was a forged or fabricated or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.
For that matter, no suggestion was given even to the effect that the PA report or intimation letter were never received by it.
Thus, accused cannot take benefit on this count.
The accused has virtually accepted, having chosen not to deny, the fact that the PA report was sent through registered post.
16. Once this fact of sending the letter is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
It is not the case of the accused that the said letter Ex. PW-4/A was sent at an incorrect address.
No such stand has been taken by the accused at any stage of trial including prosecution evidence, statement of accused or defence evidence.
This address, which is the admittedly correct address, is the same address at which the intimation letter was sent to it.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post at a correct and proper address,
there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.
The burden would not upon be the complainant
to show delivery of the letter and such Da vs Sanjay Kumar on 2 August, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/67851671/
4 burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
But the accused has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by it to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letter was delivered or if it remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not delivered to the accused.
DA vs Sanjay Kumar Accused has not claimed that its office had been shifted or closed or that the letter could not have been served upon it otherwise at the relevant time.
Thus, accused has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
Therefore, it is held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused in due course.
The accused cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things at the stage of final arguments and claim for the first time that PA report was not received by it.
17. Further it would be no defence available to the accused to claim that he was not the manufacturer of the commodity in question or that he was only a retailer using the same.
A seller or packer or distributor or manufacturer would operate in different fields and all of them can be held liable in their separate areas.
Sale of adulterated food article is prohibited.

The definition of 'sale'
under section 2 (xiii) is very wide which includes storing or exposing for sale as a retailer and even attempt to sell and also sale for analysis.

The only benefit which the accused can claim on this ground is under section 19(2) of PFA Act which would apply only if he is able to show that he had purchased the product against a warranty and had been selling the product in the same manner as purchased by him which is not the case here.

18. The case in hand would be therefore covered under section 2(ia)
(a) of PFA Act as there is evidence to show that it was not of the nature, substance or quality which it is purported to be as per PFA Rules.
The case would fall under section 2(ia)(j) as there is presence of colour which is not permitted in this article.

Violation DA vs Sanjay Kumar of section 2(ia)(j) is punishable under section 16(1A) and violation of section 2(ia)(a) is punishable under section 16(i)(a)
of PFA Act.
But being graver offence, conviction can be under section 16(1A) of PFA Act.
19. Having said so, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused had sold adulterated food in violation of section 2(ia)(a) and (j) of PFA Act read with Rules 23, 28 and 29 of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1A) of PFA Act.
20.
Thus, the accused is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1A) of the PFA Act.
Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence..

Announced in the open court this 02nd day of August 2018 SAMAR VISHAL ACMM-II (New Delhi),
